metaDescription: Seven handheld blower-vacuum-mulchers compared by airflow, mulch ratio, bag size and power source, so you can pick one that clears your yard.
expertTake: The WORX WG509 is the best all-round handheld leaf vacuum because its 18:1 mulch ratio and tidy tool-free conversion beat the corded rivals. The Heywork 450 CFM corded model is the value pick for a small lot with an outlet nearby. Skip the category if your yard is mostly heavy wet leaves on a big lot, because a 40 liter bag fills too fast to be efficient there.
introParagraphs: A handheld leaf vacuum is a blower that reverses its job: the fan pulls leaves in through a tube, a metal or plastic impeller chops them, and a zip bag catches the shredded result. The reward is fewer bags to haul to the curb and mulch that composts quickly.

The compromise is weight and workflow. You carry the motor and a full bag on one shoulder strap, and the tube is shorter than a rake handle. These machines suit patios, flower beds, decks and small lawns far better than open acreage.

products.name: WORX Trivac WG509 12 Amp 3-in-1, 350 CFM, 18:1 mulch
products.description:
The Trivac is built around a single 12 amp motor that serves all three jobs, so conversion between blowing and vacuuming is a matter of swapping a tube and fitting the bag. That is the reason it stays so manageable in the hand: there is no battery pack hanging off the housing and no fuel tank to balance. Its 18:1 mulch ratio is the highest of the corded machines in this lineup, which means a heap of leaves shrinks to a small fraction of its original bulk before it reaches the bag.

The tradeoff is airflow. At 350 CFM it moves less air than the Heywork 450 CFM, so its blowing mode will push a pile more slowly. What you get in return is air speed of 210 MPH, which is helpful for lifting matted leaves out of mulch beds and for scraping wet debris off a patio. It is the model to buy if the job is mostly vacuum and mulch rather than moving big drifts across a lawn.

The cord is the real ownership constraint. Plan on a 50 foot, heavy gauge outdoor extension cord, because a thin cord causes voltage drop and a hot motor. After each session pull the bag, shake out the fine dust, and clear the intake screen of stringy debris, since a partly blocked inlet is the usual reason mulchers lose suction.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with a small to mid yard and an outlet within cord reach who want the best mulch reduction.
pros: Highest mulch ratio of the corded group
Tool-free swap between blower and vacuum
No battery cost or runtime limit
210 MPH speed lifts matted leaves
cons: Lower airflow than the 450 and 530 CFM rivals
Cord limits reach and snags on shrubs
Bag fills quickly on heavy wet leaves

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 3-in-1 12 Amp, 230 MPH, vortex impeller
products.description:
This is the classic homeowner design, and the thing that sets it apart is the vortex-style impeller that the maker says resists clogging while mulching. In practice that matters most with sticky, damp leaves, which tend to wad up around a plain blade and choke the tube. The housing converts without tools, and the whole unit is simple enough that spare parts and replacement bags are easy to find.

At 230 MPH it has the fastest quoted air speed of the corded handhelds here, a few miles per hour above the WORX WG509 at 210. The maker quotes a 10-to-1 bag reduction, which is a lower compression than the WORX at 18:1, so you will empty the bag more often. That makes it a better fit for light, dry leaf cleanup than for dense piles.

Upkeep is short: unplug it, empty the bag, wipe out the impeller housing, and keep the cord coiled loosely rather than tightly wrapped. The impeller is plastic-bladed in this class, so pulling twigs and small stones out of the pile before you vacuum extends its life. Store it hung up with the bag removed so the fabric dries and does not mildew.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a familiar corded design with simple, replaceable consumables.
pros: Anti-clog impeller helps with damp leaves
Fast quoted air speed for loosening debris
Converts without tools
Parts and bags are widely stocked
cons: Lower mulch compression means frequent emptying
Plastic-bladed mulcher dislikes twigs and stones

products.name: Heywork 3-in-1 Corded Leaf Vacuum, 450 CFM, 40L bag
products.description:
Heywork puts the emphasis on volume rather than speed. Its 450 CFM figure is the highest airflow of any corded vacuum-mulcher in this lineup in the corded group, and it trades that for a lower 158 MPH air speed. The result is a machine that moves a larger air column gently, which suits sweeping a lawn's leaf scatter more than blasting stuck debris out of cracks.

A 40 liter bag with a 15:1 mulch ratio is sensible capacity for a handheld, and it sits between the BLACK+DECKER's 10:1 claim and the WORX's 18:1. Pick it when the budget is tight and the yard is flat and open. Expect to give up the polish of a long-established brand, so read the listing carefully for the warranty terms and the replacement bag availability before you buy.

The corded motor demands the same discipline as any plug-in unit: use a proper outdoor cord, keep the plug connection off wet grass, and never vacuum standing water or wet clumps that could reach the motor. Clean the intake mesh and the mulching chamber after each use, and let the bag dry fully before folding it away.
products.bestFor: Budget-minded owners of a flat, open small lawn with outlet access.
pros: High 450 CFM airflow for the cost tier
40 liter bag is a practical size
15:1 mulch ratio cuts bag count well
Simple corded design without batteries
cons: 158 MPH speed trails the 210 and 230 MPH rivals
Less proven service network than the big brands

products.name: MZK 40V Brushless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher, 700 CFM, 40L bag
products.description:
MZK is the cordless option that frees you from the extension cord, and its brushless motor is what keeps heat and wear down. The headline 700 CFM is the highest airflow in this guide, but note the maker ties the turbo mode to a 10 second burst, which tells you the figure is a peak, not a number you will hold continuously. Its internal suction tube and square connector are designed to keep leaves from catching at the joints, a common jam point on handhelds.

The cordless layout changes the weighing. You gain mobility around trees, sheds and flower beds, but runtime is limited by the pack, and the listing does not make clear what battery comes in the box, so verify that before buying. Against the Greenworks 48V, which uses two 24V packs and a 520 CFM rating, the MZK has higher peak airflow but a lesser known brand behind it.

Batteries are the long-term cost. Keep packs out of the cold and heat, store them partly charged, and do not leave them in the tool over winter. Clean the vacuum tube joints after each use because stray twig fragments here are what start a jam.
products.bestFor: Owners who want cordless freedom and high peak airflow without a cord.
pros: No cord to drag or snag
Brushless motor runs cooler
Anti-jam suction tube design at the joints
40 liter bag with tool-free modes
cons: Turbo is only a 10 second burst
Battery contents need checking on the listing
Runtime shortens on heavy wet leaves

products.name: Greenworks 48V (24V x 2) 520 CFM Leaf Vacuum, 4.0Ah x 2
products.description:
Greenworks pairs two 24V batteries to make a 48V system, and the numbers it quotes are the best balanced of the cordless group: 520 CFM and 240 MPH together. That air speed is the highest of any machine in this lineup, which makes it the most effective at pulling stubborn wet leaves off pavement. The brushless motor and included dual-port charger are aimed at keeping a long session going without waiting on a single pack.

Compared with the MZK, the Greenworks gives up some peak airflow, 520 versus 700, but its two 4.0Ah packs are a known quantity in the box. Greenworks batteries also fit across the maker's other 24V tools, which lowers the long-term cost if you already own some. The weight of two packs is worth thinking about for a handheld you hold at arm's length.

Care is straightforward but matters. Rotate the two packs, store them indoors at partial charge, and wipe the battery contacts if you see corrosion. Clean the impeller housing each session, because leaf sap builds up on the blades over a season and slowly reduces suction.
products.bestFor: Users who want the strongest cordless blowing and can share batteries across Greenworks tools.
pros: 240 MPH is the top speed in this guide
Two batteries and fast charger included
Brushless motor holds up under load
Packs interchange with other 24V tools
cons: Two packs add noticeable carry weight
Peak CFM trails the 700 CFM MZK

products.name: ECHO ES-250 25.4cc Gas Shred N Vac
products.description:
The ES-250 is the only gas machine in this roundup and the only one that works in the middle of a field with no outlet and no battery to run down. A 25.4cc two-stroke engine is a small-displacement power plant, built to be light enough to carry while still driving the fan and shredding impeller. Variable speed control lets you lower the throttle for delicate beds and open it up for driveway sweeping.

The tradeoff is the usual gas story. It is louder than any of the electric models, it vents exhaust, and it needs premixed fuel, so it demands more of the owner than a plug-in does. The listing does not give CFM or MPH figures, so you cannot compare its airflow numerically with the 700 CFM MZK or 520 CFM Greenworks; judge it by the engine class and the brand's reputation for starting reliably.

Expect proper two-stroke upkeep: fresh premix, a clean air filter, a spark plug checked every season, and a drained or stabilized fuel tank before winter. Letting old mixed fuel sit in the carburetor is the most common reason a small gas blower will not start in spring.
products.bestFor: Users with no power access who accept two-stroke maintenance.
pros: No cord, no battery runtime limit
Works anywhere on the property
Variable speed control
Established ECHO engine line
cons: No published CFM or MPH to compare
Needs premix fuel and seasonal upkeep

buyingCriteria.explanation: A mulch ratio tells you how much bag volume you save, because shredded leaves pack down far smaller than whole ones. The WORX WG509 quotes 18:1, the Heywork quotes 15:1, and the BLACK+DECKER quotes up to 10 bags into 1. Do not assume the highest number is always better, because a high ratio only holds if the impeller can chew through the actual leaf type you have. Dry oak leaves shred well, while sticky wet maple clumps can drop that ratio sharply.

Corded models such as the WORX and Heywork give unlimited runtime but are limited by the extension cord, which should be a heavy gauge outdoor cord of no more than about 50 feet. Cordless models such as the MZK and Greenworks add freedom but each pack gives a short window at full output. If your longest run from an outlet is under about 100 feet and you have few obstacles, corded is cheaper and simpler. Choose cordless when the yard has beds, trees or fences that tangle a cord.

CFM measures how much air moves, while MPH measures how fast it moves, and a vacuum needs both. The MZK at 700 CFM and 180 MPH is volume heavy, while the Greenworks at 520 CFM and 240 MPH leans on speed. Volume helps sweep a wide leaf field and carry leaves up the tube; speed helps break wet leaves loose from the ground. Peak figures are measured at the nozzle without the bag attached, so real vacuum performance is always lower.

A 40 liter bag, as found on the MZK and Heywork, sounds roomy, but the bag is on your shoulder and gets heavy as it fills. Mulching reduces bulk but not weight, and wet leaves weigh far more than dry ones. Plan on stopping to empty it every few minutes in a heavy leaf fall. A zippered or wide-open bag bottom makes emptying fast; a narrow neck makes it a chore.

Handhelds are used at an angle, and the vacuum tube is short, so you will bend or use a longer reach when working lawn. The shoulder strap matters more than any spec sheet number. Look for a strap that lets the motor sit at hip level and a handle that balances with the bag partly full. A heavy front-loaded motor causes wrist strain after 15 minutes.

The mulching impeller is a wear part: stones, nails and twigs chip it. The BLACK+DECKER and WORX have commonly stocked replacement bags and impellers, while newer brands like Heywork are riskier on parts supply. Gas models such as the ECHO ES-250 need fuel, plugs and filters on top of that. Check parts availability before you buy a model, not after the bag tears.

specDecoder.meaning: Cubic feet per minute of air leaving the nozzle in blower mode. It measures volume of air, not suction power.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MZK's 700 CFM is a peak figure, and the maker pairs it with a 10 second turbo burst.

specDecoder.meaning: The speed of air at the tip of the tube. It decides how well a blower lifts debris stuck to the ground.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks 240 MPH leads this lineup, while the Heywork at 158 MPH is notably slower.

specDecoder.meaning: How many bags of whole leaves fit into one bag of shredded leaves. It is a volume reduction figure that depends on leaf dryness and impeller design.
specDecoder.watchFor: WORX claims 18:1 while the BLACK+DECKER quotes about 10:1, so bag size differs in practice.

specDecoder.meaning: Current draw of a corded motor at full load, a rough proxy for power. Voltage is fixed at household 120V so amps tell you the motor class.
specDecoder.watchFor: Both the WORX and BLACK+DECKER are 12 Amp, so differences come from fan and impeller design, not raw power.

specDecoder.meaning: Voltage is the platform, amp-hours are the fuel tank. A 48V pack system built from two 24V packs adds voltage and runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks includes two 4.0Ah packs; the MZK listing needs a check for what battery is included.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mechanism and impeller design
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated how each machine reduces leaves, from the vortex impeller on the BLACK+DECKER to the six-blade layout described for other brands. A cleaner impeller path means less clogging with damp leaves. We favored designs that let material feed straight through rather than snagging at joints.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow and speed balance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared quoted CFM and MPH across the lineup, from the 350 CFM and 210 MPH WORX to the 700 CFM MZK. A strong vacuum needs both volume and speed, so models skewed heavily to one were marked down. Peak numbers were treated as ceilings, not guarantees.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bag capacity and mulch ratio
howWeEvaluated.description: Bag size and reduction ratio together decide how often you stop. Ratings from 10:1 up to 18:1 and 40 liter bags were weighed against each other. We rewarded designs that make emptying quick.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and parts
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we looked at how easy it is to find replacement bags and impellers and whether the power source adds upkeep. Gas, battery and cord each carry different long-term burdens. Brand service history counted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across power sources
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the cost of entry in relative tiers, then adjusted for what you must add: a cord, extra batteries, or fuel. A cheap corded unit may cost less over its life than a cordless one that needs a second pack.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The WORX WG509, BLACK+DECKER, and Heywork never run down and need no battery replacement. Their limit is the cord reach and the tripping hazard it creates. You also lose the ability to work during a power cut.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The MZK and Greenworks let you walk anywhere and avoid cord tangles around shrubs. Runtime is limited by pack capacity, and a spare pack is a real extra cost. Battery wear will eventually need a replacement.

howToChoose.note: Pick corded for small, open yards near an outlet; pick cordless when the yard is cluttered or far from power.

rows: Brushless motor, quiet compared with gas

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An impeller that resists clogging and high air speed to lift leaves stuck to the ground. Wet leaves weigh far more than dry ones, so expect to empty the bag faster and expect lower effective suction than the spec sheet shows.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks 48V at 240 MPH and the BLACK+DECKER with its anti-clog vortex impeller are best for damp debris. The Heywork at 158 MPH is the weaker choice for sticking leaves.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You have a mid-size yard, want cordless freedom, or plan to use the battery platform across other tools. The Greenworks 48V and MZK 40V reward that. The mulch quality of the WORX is also worth the extra.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your yard is small, flat and near an outlet. The Heywork 450 CFM will do the job, and the saved money can go to a better extension cord.

maintenance.why: Damp leaf dust grows mildew and clogs the fabric pores. A dry bag keeps suction up and prevents odor.
Stringy debris and bark choke the airflow and heat the motor. A clear screen preserves both suction and motor life.
Chips and bent blades cause vibration and poor mulching. Replace a damaged impeller before it breaks free.
A frayed cord is a shock risk, and corroded battery terminals cause voltage drop. Fix early.
Batteries should sit partly charged indoors, and the ES-250 needs its fuel drained or stabilized. Storage mistakes kill more tools than use.

faq.q: Is a leaf vacuum better than a blower and rake?
faq.a: For small, tidy areas such as patios and beds, yes, because you collect and shred in one pass. For large lawns a blower and a mower with bagger is faster. Handheld vacuums are a cleanup tool, not a primary leaf-removal system.

faq.q: How much should I spend on a handheld leaf vacuum?
faq.a: The cheapest tier here are the corded Heywork model, while the cordless Greenworks and MZK sit higher. Pay more only if you need cordless freedom or a specific mulch ratio. A good extension cord matters more than the last bit of airflow.

faq.q: How long will the mulcher last?
faq.a: The impeller is a wear part, and plastic ones wear faster when you vacuum twigs and gravel. With clean leaves and regular cleaning, most owners get several seasons. Replace the impeller, not the whole machine, when it chips.

faq.q: Does higher CFM mean better vacuum suction?
faq.a: Not directly. CFM is a blower rating measured at the nozzle without the bag. Vacuum performance depends on the intake path and the impeller, so a 350 CFM WORX can outperform a higher-rated blower at actually picking up leaves.

Damp leaves, yes, but heavy soaked piles clog the impeller and fill the bag very quickly. Never vacuum standing water on a corded model, because the motor is not sealed for liquids. Let leaves drain or dry a bit when possible.

faq.q: Are cordless leaf vacuums safe to leave on a charger?
faq.a: Use the charger that came with the tool and avoid leaving packs on it for weeks. Store them indoors at a partial charge, away from heat. Follow the battery maker's instructions.
